en: The Treatise on the True Theory of the King’s Law,
composed by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
As it is said in the sutra spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, for King Udrāyaṇa:
At one time, that king went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!...”
If a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa were to come to me and reproach or admonish me with untruthful faults appearing before me,
at that time my mind would give rise to no regret, vexation, or sorrow.
Why is this? Because when I examine these faults, I do not perceive them within myself at all.
Furthermore, there may be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who come to me and praise and exhort me with qualities that are not real.
At that time, my mind did not give rise to joy or exultation. Why was this?
Because, when observing these merits, I saw none of them within myself at all.
After those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas had departed, I dwelt alone in a secluded and quiet chamber, giving rise to this thought and engaging in deliberation and investigation:
"How should I come to know the true faults and true virtues of kings?"
"If I were to know [them], I would abandon my faults and cultivate virtue.
Which śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa is able to discern the true faults and true virtues of kings, and can also extensively explain them to me?"
Having thus reflected and investigated, he then thought:
"Only my Blessed One, the All-Knowing and All-Seeing, will certainly understand the true faults and true virtues of all these kings."
"I shall now go to the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to inquire about this meaning.
Therefore, I have now come to the Buddha's presence to request a definitive resolution of this matter.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will reveal it to me.
World-Honored One!
What are the true faults of kings?
And what are the true merits of kings?
Having made this request,
the World-Honored One then addressed King Nimi, saying: "Great King!

Great King, you should now thoroughly understand the faults of a king, the virtues of a king, the doors of a king’s decline, the doors of a king’s skillful means, the qualities dear to a king, and that which can induce those qualities dear to a king.
"What are called the faults of a king?

Great King, you should know that there are briefly nine kinds of faults of a king. If a king possesses such faults, even though he has great treasuries, great ministers, and a great army, he is not worthy of being relied upon or revered."

What are the nine? First, lack of self-mastery; second, an inherently violent and evil nature; third, the eruption of intense fury; fourth, extreme meagerness in bestowing favors; fifth, accepting the words of the wicked and sycophants; sixth, acting without reflection and disregarding established rules; seventh, having no regard for wholesome dharmas; eighth, lacking discernment and forgetting past kindnesses; ninth, being entirely unrestrained and exclusively given to negligence.
"What is meant by a king who lacks sovereignty?

It refers to a king whose disposition is not firm and whose actions are weak; he is constrained by his ministers, counselors, state preceptors, and various officials. He cannot perform the duties he ought to perform according to his own will, such as bestowing gifts upon his ministers, nor can he enjoy himself as he desires amidst the five exquisite sensual pleasures. This is what is meant by a king who lacks sovereignty."
"What is meant by a king who is violent and cruel by nature?

It refers to a king who, when his ministers or other persons commit even a minor act of disobedience in any matter, immediately confronts them with dismissal, utters coarse and evil words, and remains in a state of fierce anger and resentment with a frowning brow;
or, even if not confronting them face-to-face, he turns away from them toward others and performs acts such as dismissing or reviling them as if they were before him."
Even if one does not face the other person nor turn one's back toward them while looking elsewhere, yet performs acts such as reviling or disparaging them before them;

nevertheless, it is merely through internal mental anger and resentment, harboring a mind of malice and harm, and harboring a mind of enmity and hatred, without maintaining that state of angry resentment continuously and without relinquishing it for a long duration.

Furthermore, there is internal mental resentment and agitation; harboring a mind of malice and harm, and harboring a mind of enmity, one also maintains this state of resentment for a long time, continuing it without relinquishing it.

Due to being violent in the presence of others, violent behind their back, violent in their resentment, violent for a short duration, and violent for a long duration—this is called the king’s nature of being violent by disposition.
"Great King, you should know that long-term violence and cruelty are called a great transgression, and nothing else.
What is meant by a king who is prone to fierce outbursts of anger?

It refers to a king who, when his ministers commit even a minor fault or a slight transgression, immediately strips them of their fiefs and emoluments, seizes their wives and concubines, or punishes them with severe penalties; this is what is meant by a king who is prone to fierce outbursts of anger."
"What is meant by a king whose favors are meager?

It refers to a king whose ministers and attendants serve him with extreme purity and act in a way that is well-pleasing to his mind, yet he consoles them only with weak and feeble words; he bestows ranks, emoluments, and rewards for their meritorious services in a manner that is neither complete nor according to established custom. Or, having first depleted, delayed, evaded, or provoked resentment [regarding these gifts], he finally grants them. This is what is meant by a king whose favors are meager."
"What is meant by a king accepting the words of the wicked and sycophantic?

If there is a king who listens to and places his trust in the advice and counsel presented by certain ministers who are actually not wise but falsely appear to be wise, who are greedy, corrupt, and partisan, who are unacquainted with the laws and regulations, who harbor intentions of rebellion, and who do not cultivate good governance—due to these causes and conditions, the king’s affairs, wealth, reputation, and virtuous administration all decline; this is what is meant by a king accepting the words of the wicked and sycophantic."
"What is meant by a king acting without reflection and contrary to established rules?

It refers to a king who, regarding his various ministers, fails to investigate and fails to investigate thoroughly, and fails to deliberate and fails to deliberate carefully; he entrusts those unfit for the confidential matters of various affairs with such duties, while failing to entrust those who are fit; he fails to employ those fit for service, yet employs those unfit for service; he punishes those who deserve rewards, and rewards those who deserve punishment."

Furthermore, when he fails to properly establish his ministers in the traditional protocols of former kings, because of this, when those ministers are present at great assemblies, they interrupt the flow of discourse before others have finished speaking; they fail to show respect or restraint while offering counsel and debate; they do not properly carry out his instructions as intended; and they do not correctly abide by the king’s commands. This is called the king acting without reflection and being unaccordant with established protocol.
"What is meant by a king who disregards the wholesome Dharma?
It refers to a king who does not believe in other worlds and lacks understanding of them.

Because he neither believes nor understands in other worlds, he is unable to have faith or comprehension regarding the future results—whether pleasant or unpleasant—of wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions."

Because he lacks faith and understanding, he is devoid of shame; he engages in the three types of unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind according to his own whims. He is unable to practice giving and cultivate merit from time to time, nor does he observe the fast or train in the precepts. This is what is meant by a king who disregards wholesome dharmas.
"What is meant by a king who is ignorant of distinctions and forgets favors received?

It refers to a king whose mind is inverted regarding his ministers, counselors, state preceptors, and various officials, such that he does not properly discern their differences in terms of loyalty, skill, and wisdom."

Because of ignorance, one conceives the notion of faithfulness toward that which is not faithful, and the notion of unfaithfulness toward that which is faithful; one conceives the notion of skill toward that which lacks skill, and the notion of lack of skill toward that which possesses skill; one conceives the notion of wholesome wisdom toward that which is unwholesome wisdom, and the notion of unwholesome wisdom toward that which is wholesome wisdom.

Due to such a perversion of mind, he honors, respects, cherishes, and supports ministers who are disloyal, unskilled, and of evil wisdom, while conversely treating with contempt and disdain those ministers who are loyal, skilled, and of excellent wisdom.

Furthermore, when ministers have grown old and infirm, having served and attended him throughout the long night, yet he recognizes them as being without power, strength, or valor, and consequently ceases to respect or love them, fails to grant them rank or emolument, and does not reward their services; even if they are treated with contempt, he neglects them and takes no account of them—this is called a king who lacks discernment and forgets the kindnesses he has received.
"What is meant by a king who is entirely self-indulgent and exclusively given to negligence?

It refers to a king who is completely immersed in the five excellent sensual pleasures, becoming addicted to them, delighting in play, and finding enjoyment in their practice; he is unable from time to time to exert himself through skillful means to perform his duties or to reward his ministers. This is what is meant by a king who is entirely self-indulgent and exclusively given to negligence."
"If there is a king who possesses these nine kinds of faults, although he has great treasuries, great ministers, and a great army, he is not to be relied upon or revered."
"Great King, you should know that these nine faults are the inherent faults of a king.
What are called the virtues of a king?
Great King, you should know that the virtues of a king are, in brief, of nine kinds."
If a king accomplishes such virtues, he is worthy of being relied upon and revered even though he lacks great treasuries, lacks great ministers, and lacks a great army.
What are these nine?

First, attaining great mastery; second, having a nature free from violence and malice; third, having slight outbursts of anger; fourth, possessing intense benevolence; fifth, accepting upright speech; sixth, reflecting deeply on all actions to ensure they accord with proper decorum; seventh, cherishing wholesome dharmas; eighth, skillfully discerning distinctions and recognizing the kindness of others' deeds; ninth, not being self-indulgent and refraining from negligence.
"What is meant by a king attaining great sovereignty?

It refers to a king who, according to his own desires, performs what ought to be done and bestows rewards upon his ministers; who enjoys and sports in the five sublime sensual pleasures; and whose every command issued to his high ministers, chief counselors, state preceptors, and the assembly of officials is proclaimed without obstruction. This is called a king attaining great sovereignty."
"What is meant by a king who is not violent or cruel by nature?

It refers to a king for whom, even when his various ministers commit acts that are excessively disagreeable in any respect, he is naturally able to endure them; he does not openly dismiss or banish them, nor does he speak out or become enraged. To speak more fully, he does not give way to outbursts of anger;

he does not confront them face-to-face nor turn his back on them to carry out such actions; he does not harbor resentment within his mind, nor does he maintain a continuous stream of malice and indignation through the long night without letting it go."
He does not manifest cruelty, does not turn his back on cruelty, does not conceal cruelty, and does not persist in cruelty; this is called a king whose nature is not cruel.
What is meant by a king whose outbursts of anger are slight?

It means that there may be a king who, even though his various ministers and officials commit great offenses or grave transgressions, does not strip them all of their fiefs and emoluments, nor seize their wives and concubines, nor punish them with severe penalties.
To impose demotion and punishment according to the gravity of the offense—this is called a king whose indignation is slight.
What is meant by a king whose favors are intense? It refers to a king whose ministers serve and attend him with integrity;

their minds are pure and their dispositions are harmonious. From time to time, the king consoles them with upright, perfect, and gentle words, and bestows upon them fully endowed ranks, emoluments, and rewards for their services. He does not cause them to suffer depletion, delay, exhaustion, or resentment; they are easy to serve and not difficult to attend upon. This is called a king whose favors are intense.
"What is meant by a king who accepts upright speech?

It refers to a king who, when his ministers and officials are truly wise yet free from pride regarding their wisdom, untainted and impartial, well-versed in the legal codes, loyal in heart and intent on practicing wholesome dharmas—listens to, accepts, and puts into practice the counsel and deliberations offered by such persons. By reason of this, the affairs of state, wealth, reputation, and wholesome dharmas all flourish; this is what is meant by a king who accepts upright speech."
"What is meant by a king who acts with careful reflection and in accordance with proper protocol?

It refers to a king who, by nature, is capable of investigation and thorough investigation, and by nature, is capable of discernment and thorough discernment regarding his various ministers. In matters of state and confidential affairs, he does not entrust those unfit for such trust, but entrusts those who are fit; he does not employ those unfit for labor, but employs those who are fit; he properly rewards those who deserve reward, and properly punishes those who deserve punishment."
In all his actions, he deliberates and discriminates thoroughly before acting, never acting with haste or violence.

Furthermore, he is able to ensure that his ministers properly observe the protocols established by the former kings; consequently, even when attending banquets, these ministers never interrupt the ongoing discourse with their own speech, but rather wait for the speaker to conclude before respectfully and reverently offering counsel or remonstrance.
If one skillfully practices according to the intent of his instructions and is able to dwell correctly in accordance with the king’s commands,
this is called a king who acts with careful reflection and in full conformity with proper protocol.
"What is meant by a king’s regard for and attachment to wholesome dharmas?
It refers to a king who has faith and knowledge of the next world.
Because he has faith in what is wholesome, he is able to correctly believe and understand the pure and impure karmas, as well as their pleasant and unpleasant fruits, in the future."

By virtue of faith and understanding, being endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, he does not indulge his passions in committing the three types of unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind; from time to time, he reflects and chooses to practice generosity, cultivate merit, observe the fast, and train in the precepts. This is what is meant by a king who looks back with affection toward the wholesome Dharma.
"What is meant by a king who is skilled in discerning distinctions and recognizes the kindness he has received?

It refers to a king who, regarding his ministers, counselors, state preceptors, and various officials, possesses a mind free from delusion and is able to clearly discern their differences in terms of loyalty and integrity, technical skill, and wisdom."

Whether the various ministers possess loyalty, integrity, skill, and wisdom, or lack them, he knows each as it truly is; those who lack these qualities he treats with slight and keeps at a distance, while those who possess them he honors and loves, receiving them with proper care.

Furthermore, as for the various ministers who have grown old and infirm, having served and protected [the sovereign] throughout the long night, although he knows they are now without power, strength, or valor, he remembers their past kindness and instead conceives feelings of reverence and affection rather than contempt; he continues to bestow upon them their ranks, emoluments, and rewards for meritorious service without fail.
This is called a king who well understands distinctions and recognizes the kindness he has received.
What is meant by a king who does not indulge himself and does not act with negligence?

It refers to a king who, regarding the five excellent sensual pleasures, does not sink into them, nor become attached to them, nor revel in them, nor take delight in their practice; yet, from time to time, he exerts himself through skillful means to perform what ought to be done and bestows rewards upon his ministers. This is called a king who does not indulge himself and does not act with negligence.
"If a king is endowed with such virtues, he is worthy of veneration even if he possesses no great treasury, no great ministers, and no great army."
"Great King, you should know that these nine kinds of royal virtues are the inherent virtues of a king.
What, then, are called the doors of a king's decline?"
Great King, you should know that there are briefly five ways in which a king suffers decline:
first, appointing ministers without careful examination;
second, although he has examined them well, he fails to treat his ministers with kindness and sublime conduct, or even if he does, it is not at the proper time.
Third, they are exclusively devoted to negligence and do not attend to their administrative duties;
fourth, they are exclusively devoted to negligence and do not guard the treasuries;
fifth, they are exclusively devoted to negligence and do not practice the Dharma.
These five kinds are all termed "gates of decline for a king.
What is meant by a king who governs his ministers without proper investigation?

It refers to a king who, regarding his ministers and officials, fails to examine them thoroughly and fails to investigate them with care; he does not discern or carefully deliberate upon their distinctions in terms of loyalty, skill, and wisdom. Yet, he takes them as personal attendants, bestows affection upon them, grants them generous titles and emoluments, awards them heavy rewards for their services, entrusts them with the most confidential matters, and frequently consoles them with gentle words.

However, the wealth and treasures entrusted to these ministers are largely squandered; when they encounter enemies or hostile armies, they are the first to retreat and flee in fear and disarray, being defeated by others; lagging behind the rest, they flee without any sense of loyalty, resorting to deceitful and evil schemes that disrupt the administration of the king’s governance.
This is called a king who gathers his ministers without careful examination.
What is meant by a king who, despite examining them well, gathers his ministers without acts of kindness or skillful conduct, even if such acts are performed at improper times?

It refers to a king who, although by nature capable of investigating and thoroughly investigating, and by nature capable of discerning and thoroughly discerning the distinctions among his ministers regarding their loyalty, skill, and wisdom, does not take them as close attendants out of affection; nor does he bestow ranks and emoluments upon them according to their merit, nor entrust them with the most confidential matters, nor frequently address them with gentle words or manifest signs of consolation.

At one time, when the king encountered an enemy or a hostile army of evil friends—and as has been explained at length—until such great terrors and life-threatening dangers were present before him, it was then that he showed favor and affection toward his ministers, and as has been explained at length, even repeatedly comforted them with gentle words.
At that time, the ministers said to one another:
"The King, due to his current state of peril and urgency, is merely practicing these excellent deeds toward us for the moment; it is not out of a long-term intention."
Having understood this, although he possesses loyalty, integrity, skill, and wisdom, he keeps them hidden and does not manifest them.
This is called a king who, despite being skilled in observation, fails to provide kindness and wondrous conduct to his ministers, even if they are present at the proper time.
"What is meant by a king who exclusively practices negligence and does not attend to his administrative duties?

It refers to a king who, regarding matters of state such as those requiring reconciliation—both those currently being undertaken and those already accomplished—does not from time to time dwell in solitude or engage in correct reflection with wise counselors to weigh and examine the means for achieving reconciliation."

In this way, regarding matters of state affairs that require severing ties, those requiring the practice of generosity, those requiring military operations, and those requiring the recruitment of powerful allies—if he does not from time to time dwell alone in seclusion or consult with wise men to properly reflect upon, weigh, and examine the means for severing ties, up to the means for recruiting powerful factions—this is called a king who exclusively practices negligence and fails to attend to his affairs of state.
"What is meant by a king who exclusively practices negligence and fails to guard his treasuries?

It refers to a king who manages his affairs poorly, manages them incompetently, does not maintain his affairs, and does not oversee his affairs; who fails to secure the royal gates, fails to secure the palace gates, and fails to secure the treasuries; and who, whether at places of actors, musicians, jesters, and frivolous entertainments, or through addiction to gambling and games, squanders his wealth and treasures beyond measure. This is what is meant by a king who exclusively practices negligence and fails to guard his treasuries."
"What is meant by a king who practices only negligence and does not cultivate the practice of the Dharma?

It refers to a king who does not frequently go to pay respects to, consult, or inquire of those śramaṇas or brahmins renowned in the world for their gentleness, sincerity, intelligence, eloquence, understanding, and liberation; for their skillful means and harmlessness; and for their delight in the dharma of non-harming:
'What constitutes the good?'"
What is unwholesome?
What is blameworthy? What is blameless?
What kind of karma can bring about auspiciousness and keep one far removed from all evils?

Even if one hears of this, if one does not exert oneself to practice according to the teaching, one will be unable to practice timely giving, plant roots of merit, observe the fasts, and train in the precepts.
This is called a king who practices exclusively in negligence and does not cultivate the practice of the Dharma.

If there is a king who possesses these five doors of decline, it should be known that this king loses the benefits of both the present life and future lives; specifically, the first four doors cause the loss of benefits in the present life, while the final door causes the loss of benefits in future lives.
"What is called the 'Gate of Royal Expedients'?
Great King, you should know that the Gate of Royal Expedients consists briefly of five kinds. What are these five?"

First, skillfully observing and gathering his ministers; second, being able to bestow gracious and wondrous deeds upon them at the proper time; third, being free from negligence and single-mindedly attending to state affairs; fourth, being free from negligence and skillfully guarding the treasury and granaries; fifth, being free from negligence and single-mindedly practicing the Dharma.
"What is meant by a king who is able to skillfully examine and gather his ministers?

It refers to a king who, regarding his ministers, is naturally capable of investigating and thoroughly examining them, and naturally capable of discerning and thoroughly discerning their distinctions in terms of loyalty, trustworthiness, skill, and wisdom; he then gathers them as his personal attendants. This is what is meant by a king who is able to skillfully examine and gather his ministers."
"What is meant by a king who is able to skillfully perform acts of grace at the proper time?

It refers to a king who, having carefully examined his various ministers, takes them into his personal service and bestows upon them affection; according to their capacity, he grants them high titles and honors, rewards them generously for their meritorious services, entrusts them with the most confidential matters, and frequently consoles and encourages them with gentle words."

On one occasion, when the king encountered the great terror of an enemy force or hostile allies and his life was in imminent danger, he exhausted all his resources to manifest his loyalty, trustworthiness, skill, and wisdom.
This is called a king who is able to skillfully perform acts of benevolence at the proper time.
What is meant by a king who is free from negligence and is single-mindedly attentive to his administrative duties?

It refers to a king who, regarding the tasks and affairs to be accomplished through conciliation and alliance, is able from time to time to dwell alone in seclusion or to engage in correct reflection together with wise men, weighing and examining the means for such reconciliation and alliance.

In this way, regarding the affairs to be accomplished through estrangement, the affairs to be accomplished through giving, the affairs to be accomplished through military arrays, and the affairs to be accomplished through winning over powerful factions—he is able from time to time, dwelling alone in seclusion or together with the wise, to correctly reflect upon, weigh, and examine the methods for estrangement, up to the methods for winning over strong factions.
This is called a king who is free from negligence and is exclusively attentive to his administrative duties.
What is meant by a king who is free from negligence and skillfully guards his treasuries?

It refers to a king who extensively undertakes enterprises, skillfully undertakes enterprises, properly maintains enterprises, and carefully inspects enterprises; who strictly secures the royal gates, strictly secures the palace gates, and strictly secures the treasuries; and who does not squander wealth and treasures in excessive measure upon actors, musicians, jesters, performers, or those seeking amusement, nor does he indulge in gambling, board games, or similar diversions.
This is called a king who is free from negligence and properly guards his treasuries.
What is meant by a king who is free from negligence and is devoted exclusively to the practice of the Dharma?

It refers to a king who frequently visits, pays homage to, and consults those śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are known in the world for their gentleness and sincerity, their wisdom and eloquence, their attainment of understanding and liberation, and their skillful means and harmlessness, as well as their delight in the dharma of non-harming.
What is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is faulty?
"What constitutes non-offensiveness?
What kind of karma can bring about auspiciousness and distance one from all evils?

Having heard this, may you be well able to exert yourselves and practice according to the teaching, and may you also from time to time practice giving to plant merit, observe the fasts, and train in the precepts."
This is called a king who is free from negligence and is exclusively devoted to the practice of the Dharma.

If a king accomplishes these five doors of skillful means, it should be known that this king does not fall away from the benefits of either the present life or future lives; specifically, by means of the first four doors he does not fall away from the benefits of the present life, and by means of the final door he does not fall away from the benefits of future lives.
"What are the qualities that are dear to a king?
Great King, you should know that there are briefly five kinds of qualities that are dear, delightful, joyful, and pleasing to kings."

What are the five? First, being respected and loved by the world; second, possessing sovereign power; third, being able to crush enemies; fourth, being able to properly nourish and maintain the body; and fifth, being able to proceed to the happy realms.
These five kinds of things are the qualities that a king finds lovely, delightful, pleasing, and agreeable.
"How does one bring about those qualities that are lovely to a king?
Great King, you should know that there are, in brief, five ways by which the qualities lovely to kings are brought about."

What are these five? First, nurturing the world through kindness; second, being fully endowed with heroic valor; third, possessing skillful means; fourth, correctly experiencing the objective realm; and fifth, diligently practicing the cultivation of the Dharma.
"What is meant by a king who nurtures the world with benevolence?

It refers to a king whose nature is fundamentally one of contentment; who, regarding the acquisition of wealth and treasures, is by nature prudent and free from improper greed or attachment; and who accumulates wealth and treasures as is appropriate, rather than seeking them out extensively."

Furthermore, there was a king whose nature was free from greed and stinginess; having accomplished the pure dharma of non-attachment, he bestowed his own treasury and precious wealth upon all who were poor, destitute, and unprotected, according to his power and ability.

Furthermore, there was a king who was gentle and patient, who frequently instructed the realm with mild words. From time to time, he bestowed ranks and emoluments upon his subjects as was appropriate; yet he never assigned to his ministers tasks that were beyond their capability, nor did he employ them in evil or grievous labors.

Regarding those offenses that deserved compassion and pardon, he immediately showed mercy; regarding those offenses that could not be pardoned, he punished them according to the facts, at the proper time, and in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, a king sustains the world through the grace of the Dharma of righteous governance.
Because the king practices such a method of sustaining the world, he consequently inspires the respect and affection of the world.
"What is meant by a king being endowed with valor?

It refers to a king who is diligent in strategy and perfect in military tactics; he subdues those not yet subdued and protects those already subdued. He extensively undertakes affairs as previously described, up to and including not being excessively addicted to gambling, board games, and the like. Furthermore, he skillfully observes what is appropriate and inappropriate regarding his officials and subjects, diligently applying punishment where it is deserved and providing care where it is required."
This is called a king being endowed with valor and heroism.
Because the king practices such dharmas of being endowed with valor and heroism, he is consequently able to attain sovereign supremacy.
"What is meant by a king’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)?

It refers to a king who, regarding the various affairs and tasks to be accomplished—ranging from those concerning peace and reconciliation as previously described, up to those concerning the acquisition of powerful allies—is able to correctly understand the means for reconciliation and peace, up to the means for acquiring strong factions."
This is what is called a king’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Because the king practices such methods of skillful means, he is able to subdue all his enemies.

"What is meant by a king’s correct enjoyment of his domain? It refers to a king who is skillfully able to calculate the increase and decrease of his treasuries; who is neither extravagant nor miserly; who maintains a state of equanimity; who enjoys pure and upright enjoyments, diverse enjoyments, and excellent enjoyments; who enjoys according to what is appropriate for each season; who enjoys together with his ministers, assistants, and relatives; who enjoys in superior locations; who enjoys while performing various musical performances; and who enjoys without any fault or transgression."

Regarding being free from transgression: when suffering from illness, one should eat what is appropriate and avoid what is inappropriate; when in good health, one should eat only after the previous meal has been digested. If food has not yet been digested, or if one suffers from diarrhea after eating, one should not eat.
When those who should share the meal are present before him, he should not eat exquisite and superior flavors alone while deceitfully excluding others.
This is called a king correctly experiencing his sensory objects.
Because the king practices such a method of correctly perceiving his objective sphere, he is thus able to skillfully sustain and nourish his own person.
What is meant by "the king diligently practicing the Dharma-observance"?
It refers to a king who is fully endowed with pure faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
What is meant by a king being "fully endowed with pure faith"?
It means that there is a king who has conviction in future lives, and who has conviction in the pure and impure actions of the future, as well as their pleasant and unpleasant fruits and maturations.
This is called a king who is endowed with pure faith.
What is meant by a king who is endowed with pure ethical discipline?
It refers to a king who stays far removed from killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the consumption of intoxicants—the various bases for negligence.
This is called a king who is fully endowed with pure ethical discipline.
What is meant by a king being fully endowed with pure learning?

It refers to a king who, regarding the meaning of the present life, the meaning of future lives, and the meanings pertaining to both the present and future lives—namely, various sublime gateways of the Dharma—listens well, receives them well, studies and recites them until they are mastered, and investigates them with single-minded devotion, seeing them well and attaining mastery.
This is called a king being endowed with pure learning.
What is meant by a king being endowed with pure renunciation?

It refers to a king who, though dwelling among a multitude ensnared by the defilement of stinginess, remains constantly pure in mind; he dwells at home far removed from the defilement of stinginess, always practicing relinquishment, extending his hand in joyful giving, delighting in the performance of sacrificial merit, and being perfect in generous charity; and at the time of giving, he always delights in impartiality.
This is called a king who is endowed with pure relinquishment.
What is meant by a king being endowed with pure wisdom?

It refers to a king who understands, as they truly are, wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, those that are blameworthy and blameless, those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated, and those that are superior or inferior, white or black. He also understands, as they truly are, the various extensively differentiated phenomena of dependent origination. Even if he should lose mindfulness and give rise to evil desire, ill will, resentment, concealment, vexation, stinginess, envy, deceit, guile, crookedness, lack of shame, lack of remorse, evil desires, or evil views, his mind awakens to them and does not remain fixed in them.
In this way, the king is said to be endowed with pure wisdom;
in this way, the king is said to be diligent in practicing the Dharma.
Because the king accepts and practices these dharmic deeds, he is able to proceed to the happy realms.

These five kinds [of qualities] are able to bring about the king’s desirable dharmas and can induce all the benefits for kings in both the present life and future lives; that is to say, the first four kinds can induce the king’s benefits in the present life, while the final kind can induce the king’s benefits in future lives.

"Furthermore, Great King, you should know that I have already briefly explained the faults of a king, the virtues of a king, the doors of a king’s decline, the doors of a king’s skillful means, the qualities dear to a king, and those qualities that can bring about what is dear to a king."

Therefore, Great King, you should practice and learn: you should distance yourself from the faults of a king and cultivate the virtues of a king; you should avoid the gates of royal decline and train in the gates of royal skillful means; you should aspire to the qualities that are dear to a king, and you should undertake the practices that can bring about those qualities dear to a king.
"Great King, if you can practice and train in this manner, you shall obtain all benefit and happiness.
Furthermore, based on the distinctions in their practice, three types of persons are established: namely, the inferior, the middling, and the superior.

One who lacks both conduct for their own benefit and conduct for the benefit of others is called an inferior person; one who possesses conduct for their own benefit but lacks conduct for the benefit of others, or possesses conduct for the benefit of others but lacks conduct for their own benefit, is called a middling person; one who possesses both conduct for their own benefit and conduct for the benefit of others is called a superior person.

Furthermore, there are four types of persons (*pudgala*): some practice evil but do not delight in evil; some delight in evil but do not practice it; some both practice evil and delight in it; and some neither practice evil nor delight in it.

If one believes that various evils can bring about undesirable retributions in the future, yet commits evil deeds due to loss of mindfulness, negligence, or association with evil friends, this is called practicing evil without delighting in evil.

If, due to having habituated oneself to evil in previous lives, one takes pleasure in various evils and is led by evil desires, yet—by relying upon associating with virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*), hearing the true Dharma, and applying correct mental attention—one perceives that various evil deeds bring about undesirable retributive fruits in the future, and thus exerts oneself and strives to distance oneself from all evils; this is called "delighting in evil but not practicing evil."
If one is by nature fond of evil and does not distance oneself from it, this is called practicing evil and also delighting in evil.
If one is by nature not fond of various evils and is also able to distance oneself from them, this is called neither practicing evil nor delighting in evil.
Among these, one who both commits evil deeds and delights in evil is called an inferior person (*hīnapuruṣa*).
One who commits evil deeds but does not delight in them, or one who delights in evil but does not commit evil deeds, is called a middling person (*madhyamapuruṣa*).
One who neither commits evil nor delights in evil is called a superior person (*uttama-puruṣa*).
Furthermore, there are three types of persons:
first, those who prioritize the enjoyment of sensual desires; second, those who prioritize worldly affairs; and third, those who prioritize the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
The first is called the inferior person, the next the middling person, and the last the superior person.
Furthermore, there are three types of individuals (*pudgala*):
first, those who take what is not their own task as their own task; second, those who take their own task as their own task; and third, those who take the tasks of others as their own task.
If one engages in unwholesome conduct to sustain oneself, it is called taking what is not one's own task as one's own task.
If, out of fear of unwholesome conduct, one practices wholesome conduct, it is called taking one's own task as one's own task.
If bodhisattvas regard the affairs of others as their own affairs and so forth—the first is called the inferior person, the next the middling person, and the last the superior person.

Furthermore, kings possess three kinds of perfection: the perfection of karmic fruition (*vipāka-saṃpad*), the perfection of human effort (*puruṣakāra-saṃpad*), and the perfection of merit (*guṇa-saṃpad*).

If kings are born into wealthy and noble families, possess long lives with few ailments, have great lineages, and are endowed with innate, sharp intelligence, such kings are said to be "perfect in karmic fruition."
If kings, being sustained by skillful means and expedient devices, constantly achieve and perfect heroic valor, such kings are said to possess the perfection of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).

If kings uphold the True Dharma, they are called Dharma Kings; if they abide securely in the True Dharma, they are called Great Kings. When such kings practice generosity together with their inner court, princes, ministers, heroes, nobles, and the people of the land, planting roots of merit, observing the fasts, and firmly maintaining the prohibitive precepts, these kings are said to be perfected in merit.
The perfection of fruition refers to the enjoyment of the results of pure karma from previous lives.
The perfection of human effort refers to the enjoyment of desirable results in the present life.
One who has perfected merit will likewise, in the future, enjoy the full fruition of the results of pure karma.
If a king lacks all three types of perfection, he is called an inferior person (*hīnapuruṣa*).
If one possesses the perfection of karmic fruition, or the perfection of human effort, or both, they are called a person of middle capacity.
If all three perfections are fully present without exception, they are called a person of superior capacity.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of ministers:

first, those who possess loyalty and integrity but lack skill and wisdom; second, those who possess loyalty, integrity, and skill but lack wisdom; and third, those who are endowed with loyalty, integrity, skill, and wisdom.
The first is called the inferior person, the next the middling person, and the last the superior person.
If one is neither loyal nor trustworthy, possesses no skillful arts, and lacks wisdom, you should know that such a minister is the lowest of the low among the inferior.
Furthermore, there are four types of speech:

first, that which is unpleasant yet appears pleasant; second, that which is pleasant yet appears unpleasant; third, that which is unpleasant and appears unpleasant; and fourth, that which is pleasant and appears pleasant.
Any speech or phrasing that is well-composed and agreeable, yet inappropriate to the occasion, is called the first type of speech.
There may be speech whose words and phrases are harsh and contrary, yet appropriate to the occasion; this is the second type of speech.
There may be speech whose words and phrases are harsh and contrary, and moreover inappropriate to the occasion; this is the third type of speech.
There may be speech whose words and phrases are skillfully harmonious and appropriate; this is the fourth type of speech.
If one proclaims that which is unlovely, that which resembles the unlovely, or speech that appears lovely though it is actually unlovely, such a person is an inferior individual.
If there is one who proclaims speech that appears pleasant but is actually unpleasant, this is a person of middling capacity.
If there is one who proclaims speech that is both pleasant and truly pleasant, this is a person of superior capacity.
Furthermore, there are three types of those who experience various sensual desires:

There are those who, driven by desire, unlawfully and recklessly amass wealth and treasures, yet are unable to provide for the comfort and proper sustenance of themselves, their wives, and their children; and so on, as extensively described, up to not cultivating the field of merit among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.

There are those who, while enjoying sensual pleasures, use wealth—whether acquired by lawful or unlawful means, and whether amassed with vigor or not—to provide for the comfort and proper maintenance of themselves, their wives, children, kinsmen, and friends, yet do not cultivate the field of merit among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.

There are those who experience sensual pleasures exclusively through the Dharma, accumulating wealth and treasures without excess or recklessness, thereby being able to maintain themselves with ease and comfort, and so forth, up to being able to cultivate fields of merit among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Among these three types, the first is called the inferior person, the second the middling person, and the last the superior person.
Furthermore, there are three other kinds of people:

the first is one who eats with greedy attachment, craving and gluttonously indulging, even becoming so addicted that they fail to see the faults [of such conduct] and do not know how to escape from it.

Second, there are those who eat with discernment, neither stained nor attached, nor gluttonous; they do not swallow greedily or consume with confusion and infatuation, but remain firm and steadfast, deeply perceiving the faults and dangers while well-knowing the way of escape, yet they have not yet abandoned nor fully understood this food.

Third, there are those who eat with discernment, giving rise to no greedy attachment; as explained at length, they even deeply perceive the faults and disadvantages [of food] and well understand the way of transcendence, and furthermore, regarding this food, they have already abandoned it and fully understood it.
The first is called the inferior person, the second the middling person, and the last the superior person.
Furthermore, based on the objects given, three types of persons are described:
first, there is the person who gives an object that possesses only exquisite fragrance, but lacks exquisite flavor and texture.
Second, there are those who give things that possess excellent fragrance and flavor but lack excellent texture.
Third, there are those who give things that are fully endowed with excellent fragrance, flavor, and texture.
The first is called the inferior person, the second the middling person, and the last the superior person.
Furthermore, based on the field of generosity (*dānakṣetra*), there are three types of persons:
first, there is the person who practices giving toward those they love and those who have been kind to them.
Second, there are those who practice giving toward the field of the poor and suffering.
Third, there are those who practice giving toward the most excellent field of merit, which is endowed with all virtues.
The first is called the inferior person, the second the middling person, and the last the superior person.

Furthermore, there are distinctions: one who gives to those they love is called an inferior person; one who gives to those who have been kind to them is called a middling person; and one who gives to the poor and suffering, or to fields of merit possessing excellence, is called a superior person.
Furthermore, based on the mind of giving, three types of persons are taught:
first, there is the person who feels joy in the mind before intending to give, yet whose mind is not pure while actually giving, and who subsequently regrets it immediately after having given.
Second, there is a person who is joyful in mind beforehand, whose mind is pure at the time of giving, but who later regrets it after having given.
Third, there is a person who is joyful in mind beforehand, whose mind is pure at the time of giving, and who has no regret after having given.
The first is called the inferior person (*hīna-pudgala*), the next the middling person (*madhya-pudgala*), and the last the superior person (*agra-pudgala*).
Furthermore, with respect to the meritorious activity of upholding the precepts, three types of persons are established:

First, there is a person who abandons only a portion [of the precepts] and is not able to remain far removed from them at all times; they distance themselves only on their own, neither exhorting others to abstain nor praising such conduct, and they do not feel joy upon seeing fellow practitioners of the Dharma. This is called the inferior person.

Second, there are those who are free from all [unwholesome] factors at all times; they distance themselves alone, neither exhorting others nor praising [such conduct], and their hearts do not rejoice upon seeing fellow practitioners of the Dharma. These are called persons of middling capacity.
Third, there are those who manifest all [qualities] together; these are called superior persons (*uttama-pudgala*).
Furthermore, regarding the observance of the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*), three types of persons are established:
first, there are those who dwell within a poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya while observing the prohibitive precepts.
Second, there are those who, dwelling within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts yet have lapses.
Third, there are those who, likewise dwelling therein, receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts without any lapses.
The first is called the inferior person (*hīna-pudgala*), the second the middling person (*madhya-pudgala*), and the last the superior person (*agra-pudgala*).
Furthermore, regarding the mind that upholds the precepts, three types of persons are established:
first, there is the person who upholds the prohibitive precepts for the sake of making a living.
Second, there are those who observe the prohibitive precepts for the sake of rebirth in heaven.
Third, there are those who observe the prohibitive precepts for the sake of nirvana.
The first is called an inferior person; the second, a middling person; and the last, a superior person.
Furthermore, regarding those who undertake the prātimokṣa vows, it is said there are three types of persons:
first, some individuals are able to undertake only the upavāsa vows;
second, some individuals are also able to undertake the upāsaka vows.
Third, there are those who are also able to receive and maintain the bhikṣu vows.
The first is called an inferior person (hīnapuruṣa), the second a middling person (madhyamapuruṣa), and the last a superior person (uttamapuruṣa).
Furthermore, regarding the reception and maintenance of the bhikṣu vows, it is said that there are three types of persons:

First, there are some persons who are able to accomplish only the factor of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), but lack the factor of receiving the various training rules (*śikṣāpada*) that accord with the Dharma, lack the factor of guarding the minds of others, and lack the factor of guarding the various training rules as they were previously received.
Second, there are those who accomplish the first three branches but lack the final one.
Third, there are those who fully accomplish all four branches.
The first is called an inferior person (*hīnapuruṣa*), the second a middling person (*madhyamapuruṣa*), and the last a superior person (*uttamapuruṣa*).
Furthermore, there are three types of persons:
first, there is the person who achieves only the prātimokṣa restraint;
second, there is the person who achieves both the prātimokṣa and dhyāna restraints.
Third, there are those who accomplish the three types of restraint: that of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The first is called an inferior person, the second a middling person, and the last a superior person.
Furthermore, there are three types of persons:
first, there is the person who is able to accomplish only the received ethical discipline (śīla-saṃvara) that is categorized as neither non-discipline nor non-non-discipline;
second, there is the person who is also able to accomplish the received ethical discipline associated with the Śrāvakas and so forth.
Third, there are those who are also able to accomplish the ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) received by a bodhisattva.
The first is called an inferior person (*hīna-puruṣa*), the second a middling person (*madhyama-puruṣa*), and the last a superior person (*uttama-puruṣa*).
Furthermore, based on the application of cultivation and reflection (*manasikāra*), three types of persons are established:
first, there is the person who attains only the "strenuous effort" mode of reflection;
second, there is the person whose reflection operates with intervals, such that even if it were to become uninterrupted, they must still apply effort for it to proceed.
Third, there are those who have already attained spontaneous contemplation (*anābhoga-manasikāra*).
The first is called the inferior person (*hīna-pudgala*), the next the middling person (*madhya-pudgala*), and the last the superior person (*adhimātra-pudgala*).
Furthermore, these three types of persons are established based on the distinctions in their attained cultivation (*bhāvanā-viśeṣa*).
First, there are those who have already attained internal mental tranquility (*śamatha*) but have not yet attained the superior wisdom of the analytical insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Second, there are those who have already attained the superior wisdom of analytical insight but have not yet attained internal mental tranquility.
Third, there are those who attain both types [of results].
The first is called an inferior person (hīnapuruṣa), the second a middling person (madhyamapuruṣa), and the last a superior person (uttamapuruṣa).
Furthermore, there are three other types of persons:
First, there are those who have already attained the samādhi with both directed thought and sustained examination.
Second, there are those who have already attained the samādhi with no directed thought and only sustained examination.
Third, there are those who have already attained the concentration (samādhi) without applied thought or sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*).
The first is called an inferior person (*hīna-puruṣa*), the second a middling person (*madhya-puruṣa*), and the last a superior person (*uttama-puruṣa*).
Furthermore, based on the distinctions in their abiding and cultivation, three types of persons are established:
first, there is the person who abides in defiled dhyāna;
second, there is the person who abides in mundane pure dhyāna.
Third, there are those who dwell in untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-dhyāna*).
The first is called an inferior person (*hīnapuruṣa*), the second a middling person (*madhyamapuruṣa*), and the last a superior person (*uttamapuruṣa*).
*Rājadharmasamyaknyāyaśāstra*, one fascicle.
